subject: Respiratory
vignette: A newborn presents with noisy breathing and cyanosis shortly after delivery. The cyanosis worsens during feeding but clearly improves when the infant cries. Examination suggests upper airway obstruction, and a nasogastric tube cannot be advanced beyond the pharynx.
question: Which of the following best explains the improvement in cyanosis during crying in this infant?

options.text: Crying increases tidal volume and recruits alveoli in the lower lobes
Crying stimulates surfactant release from type II pneumocytes
Crying closes the ductus arteriosus, improving pulmonary blood flow
Crying forces mouth breathing, bypassing the obstructed posterior nasal openings
Crying reduces pulmonary vascular resistance by raising inspired oxygen

explanation_correct: This infant has bilateral choanal atresia, a blockage of the posterior nasal openings. Because newborns are obligate nasal breathers, bilateral obstruction causes upper airway obstruction and cyanosis that worsens during feeding, when the mouth is occupied. Crying forces mouth breathing, which bypasses the blocked nasal passages and improves oxygenation. Diagnosis is by failure to pass a nasogastric tube beyond the pharynx, confirmed with CT.

explanation_incorrect.A: The improvement is not from alveolar recruitment but from switching to an oral airway that bypasses the nasal obstruction.
explanation_incorrect.B: Surfactant release is not acutely triggered by crying and would not cause an immediate change in color.
explanation_incorrect.C: Ductus arteriosus closure is unrelated to crying and would not immediately relieve an upper airway obstruction.
explanation_incorrect.E: Pulmonary vascular resistance is not the limiting problem here; the obstruction is anatomic at the posterior nasal opening.

educationalObjective: Explain why bilateral choanal atresia causes cyanosis worse with feeding and improved by crying (mouth breathing).

subject: Respiratory
vignette: A 2-day-old infant has had unilateral nasal obstruction since birth. Imaging demonstrates blockage of the posterior nasal opening together with bony abnormalities of the midface. The pediatrician tells the parents that this is the most common presentation of the condition.
question: Which of the following statements about choanal atresia is correct?

options.text: It is most often unilateral and may be associated with bony abnormalities of the midface
It most commonly affects the anterior nasal opening and presents with epistaxis
Bilateral disease is typically benign and never requires urgent intervention
It is diagnosed when a nasogastric tube passes easily beyond the pharynx
Cyanosis classically worsens during crying and improves during feeding

explanation_correct: Choanal atresia is blockage of the posterior nasal opening, most often unilateral, and is frequently associated with bony abnormalities of the midface. Unilateral cases can be subtle, whereas bilateral disease is an emergency in obligate nasal breathers. It is diagnosed by failure to pass a nasogastric tube beyond the pharynx and confirmed with CT.

explanation_incorrect.B: Choanal atresia blocks the posterior, not the anterior, nasal opening; anterior bleeding from Kiesselbach plexus is a separate entity.
explanation_incorrect.C: Bilateral choanal atresia is an emergency because of upper airway obstruction in newborns, not a benign condition.
explanation_incorrect.D: Diagnosis is suggested by failure, not success, of passing a nasogastric tube beyond the pharynx.
explanation_incorrect.E: The pattern is reversed: cyanosis worsens during feeding and improves with crying because crying is mouth breathing.

educationalObjective: Recall that choanal atresia is usually unilateral, involves the posterior nasal opening and midface bones, and is diagnosed by failed nasogastric tube passage.

subject: Respiratory
vignette: An infant with bilateral choanal atresia is evaluated for an underlying multiple-malformation syndrome. The clinical team recognizes the CHARGE association and reviews its component features with the family.
question: Which of the following findings makes up the CHARGE syndrome mnemonic?

options.text: Cataracts, Hearing loss, Alopecia, Renal agenesis, Esophageal atresia, Gastroschisis
Coloboma, Hydrocephalus, Anencephaly, Rib anomalies, Encephalocele, Gastroschisis
Cleft lip, Heart defects, Anal atresia, Radial aplasia, Esophageal fistula, Glossoptosis
Coloboma, Heart defects, Achondroplasia, Restricted growth, Hepatomegaly, Ear defects
Coloboma, Heart defects, Atresia of choanae, Restricted growth and development, Genitourinary defects, Ear defects

explanation_correct: CHARGE stands for Coloboma of the eye, Heart defects, Atresia of choanae, Restricted growth and development, Genitourinary defects, and Ear defects. Choanal atresia is a key component, so any newborn with bilateral choanal atresia should be evaluated for the full syndrome.

explanation_incorrect.A: These are not CHARGE criteria; bilateral renal agenesis belongs to Potter sequence, not this syndrome.
explanation_incorrect.B: Hydrocephalus, anencephaly, and encephalocele are neural tube or CNS defects, not features of CHARGE.
explanation_incorrect.C: This resembles other malformation associations and omits coloboma and ear defects; it is not the CHARGE mnemonic.
explanation_incorrect.D: Achondroplasia and hepatomegaly are not CHARGE features; the correct 'A' is atresia of choanae and the correct 'G' is genitourinary defects.

educationalObjective: List the six components of CHARGE syndrome and recognize choanal atresia as one of its defining features.

subject: Respiratory
vignette: A term newborn has severe respiratory distress in the delivery room with noisy breathing. Cyanosis worsens during feeding and improves when the infant cries, and a nasogastric tube cannot be advanced beyond the pharynx. The team suspects a congenital airway lesion and reviews the differential diagnosis.
question: Which of the following best explains this infant's respiratory distress?

options.text: Surfactant deficiency causing alveolar collapse, as in neonatal respiratory distress syndrome
A fistula between the trachea and esophagus formed during weeks 4 through 7
Bilateral blockage of the posterior nasal openings
A foregut budding abnormality producing a fluid-filled bronchogenic cyst
Pulmonary hypoplasia secondary to a congenital diaphragmatic hernia

explanation_correct: Cyanosis that worsens with feeding and improves with crying (mouth breathing), noisy upper-airway breathing, and failure to pass a nasogastric tube beyond the pharynx are classic for bilateral choanal atresia, a blockage of the posterior nasal openings. Because newborns are obligate nasal breathers, this is an emergency. CT confirms the diagnosis, and it may occur as part of CHARGE syndrome.

explanation_incorrect.A: Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome is surfactant deficiency with a ground-glass appearance, usually in premature infants; it would not improve with crying or block nasogastric tube passage.
explanation_incorrect.B: Tracheoesophageal fistula arises from embryonic-week errors and causes feeding-related coughing or aspiration, not the feeding-worse/crying-better pattern with a blocked nasogastric tube at the pharynx.
explanation_incorrect.D: Bronchogenic cysts are foregut budding abnormalities that are usually asymptomatic fluid-filled densities; they do not produce cyclic cyanosis relieved by crying.
explanation_incorrect.E: Pulmonary hypoplasia from congenital diaphragmatic hernia causes severe respiratory failure but not the nasal obstruction signs or failed nasogastric passage described here.

educationalObjective: Differentiate bilateral choanal atresia from other neonatal respiratory lesions using the feeding/crying cyanosis pattern and failed nasogastric tube passage.
